comparator.name: Life Science and Technology
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations specify two compulsory 60 EC years. Year three contains a 30 EC minor, 15 EC approved electives and a 15 EC research project. The degree has one major, with several permitted areas for advanced study.
components: Practical Course Optics and Cell Biology
Practical Skills in Organic Chemistry (for LST)
LST and Society: Ethical and Professional Aspects
Approved Life Science and Technology electives
Choose approved courses in biology, chemistry, biomedical engineering, medical pharmaceutical sciences or physics.
Entry requires at least 120 EC, including the complete first year. The Board of Examiners approves the project.

alternatives.label: Molecular and Biomedical Life Sciences
alternatives.labelReason: The life-science gateway precedes physiology, biochemistry, cell biology and the laboratory course. Cell and organ foundations lead into pathology, immunology, disease mechanisms and pharmacology. Statistics and data analysis support evidence interpretation.
alternatives.concept: Study how cells, molecules and organs function in health and disease. Combine cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, genetics, immunology and pharmacology with introductory laboratory and data-analysis work.
progression: The life-science gateway precedes physiology, biochemistry, cell biology and the laboratory course. Cell and organ foundations lead into pathology, immunology, disease mechanisms and pharmacology. Statistics and data analysis support evidence interpretation.

alternatives.label: Quantitative Life Sciences and Image Analysis
alternatives.labelReason: Programming precedes image processing. Mathematical Methods precedes linear algebra, numerical methods, signal analysis, statistics and Advanced Calculus. Experimental statistics precedes research synthesis. Cell biology and physiology underpin later disease study.
alternatives.concept: Study how computational methods can help investigate biological processes. Combine molecular biology and disease mechanisms with programming, statistics, numerical models, signal analysis and digital image processing.
progression: Programming precedes image processing. Mathematical Methods precedes linear algebra, numerical methods, signal analysis, statistics and Advanced Calculus. Experimental statistics precedes research synthesis. Cell biology and physiology underpin later disease study.
alternatives.distinctness: The quantitative option gives more weight to calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, statistics, signals and digital imaging. The molecular option gives more weight to organismal and nervous-system biology, anatomy and research design.

candidates.label: Quantitative Life Sciences and Image Analysis

core: Molecular and cellular biology, biochemistry, genetics and biomolecular mechanisms
Physiology, disease, pharmacology and biomedical research

questions: How do molecular and cellular processes produce biological function, disease and treatment possibilities?
How can laboratory and quantitative methods reveal cells, biomolecules and disease mechanisms?
How can mathematical and computational methods support imaging, diagnostics and biological-data analysis?

blocks: Both cover cell structure, membranes, signalling and gene regulation. UCR takes a broader molecular cell biology approach.
Both study the functions and regulation of organ systems. UCR emphasises adult human physiology.
Both study biomolecules and biochemical mechanisms. Groningen combines its course with additional chemistry requirements.
Both study genetics. UCR focuses on molecular pathology. Groningen also examines evolution.
Both introduce programming. Groningen uses life-science assignments, while UCR teaches general programming and problem solving.
Both develop calculus skills. UCR uses a general mathematical methods course.
Both study matrices, vector spaces and eigenvalues. Groningen teaches these within the Life Science and Technology curriculum.
Groningen teaches microscopy, structural imaging and medical imaging techniques. UCR’s Image Processing & Computer Vision analyses digital images.
Both include aseptic culture and microbiological techniques. The UCR course also covers other laboratory methods. Groningen has a separate microbiology practical.
Groningen teaches physical optics and microscopy.
Groningen teaches pharmaceutical analysis. UCR’s Pharmacology focuses on drug action and use.
Groningen requires a dedicated applied biotechnology course. UCR introduces selected techniques in the Life Science Laboratory.
Groningen requires an approved research project. Independent research at UCR is optional.

selection.assessment: The closest option combines molecular, physiological and disease study with laboratory work and computational methods. The second emphasises quantitative modelling and image analysis. A separate pharmacology option would reuse the same molecular, pathology and pharmacology sequence with limited medicinal chemistry. A sustainability direction would rely chiefly on ecology and environmental processes, with insufficient additional biotechnology content. Two coherent options remain.

notes.text: The UCR options focus on molecular and biomedical life sciences or on quantitative analysis. Groningen also requires a substantial sequence in chemistry, physics and specialist laboratory methods.

Groningen requires organic and bioinorganic chemistry, thermodynamics, optics, mechanics, spectroscopy, pharmaceutical analysis and specialist practicals. UCR offers related laboratory work and computational image analysis. Groningen’s 15 EC research project is compulsory.

audience.programmeDescription: Life Science and Technology at the University of Groningen combines biology, chemistry and physics to study living systems. Students complete specialist laboratory courses, a minor and a research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option focuses on molecules, cells and human health. The second adds more mathematics, computing and digital image analysis. The Groningen degree devotes substantially more time to chemistry, physics and specialist experimental methods.
